rv.q: It is enchanting to look at, but leaves us on the outside, looking in.
If you can bear the weight of that suffering, “Bughouse” makes it powerfully palpable.
A colorful tableau of a man in mental limbo, Bughouse can be an intriguing illustration, if broad-stroked, of Henry Darger as a tormented, self-mythologizing egotist.
As the lights dimmed, and perhaps after it was too late, Beckett and Bughouse were, at last, in alignment.
But if Henley and Clarke's intention is to make Darger into a compelling character, they've fallen short.

Yet despite its near-legendary creative team, its short running time and some moments of visual invention, “Bughouse” failed to keep my interest, much less convince me of Darger’s greatness in “the art brut canon” or anywhere else.
Bughouse is truly a crafting of art itself, presenting the world that surrounded Darger, unreserved honesty and sculpture.
John Kelly is awesome as an elderly outsider artist in this spellbinding solo performance piece.
But as a theater piece, it’s shockingly inert.
The production chases Darger down many dark mental corridors, but in the end, it never really finds him.
You can't say that Bughouse lacks respectable credentials, but you can say that it never truly opens the door to the obsessive imagination.
Bughouse offers a peek into one troubled creator’s mental state but fails to get to the heart of his isolation or his output.
